MathDB Lean Vocabulary

Which Mathlib definitions the Lean statements of MathDB problems are written in. Each problem counts once, however many obligations its folder publishes. Names come from Lean's elaborated terms, and what each name is comes from Lean's environment.

Definitions by number of problems

    How this was read

    Every obligation in mathdb-lean/problems was elaborated in batch against its pinned project (Lean , Mathlib , formal-conjectures ), the way Gate 0 elaborates it. From Problem.Target the walk follows every Problem.* definition the target reaches and collects the constants outside it, with Expr.getUsedConstants. A local lemma contributes its statement, not its proof.

    Lean then says what each constant is. Instances, class methods such as +, ≤ and ∈, theorems, constructors, recursors and compiler auxiliaries are left out; definitions, structures, inductive types, classes and structure fields are kept. The area is the defining module's first component under Mathlib.

    Similar problems are ranked by cosine similarity of their definition sets, each definition weighted by how rare it is, with Lean core and coercions left out. Sharing vocabulary is not sharing mathematics. Every statement here compiles; none has been read by a person against the problem's prose.

    How problems are connected

    Problem groups are Louvain communities of the graph whose edges join two problems at similarity 0.2 or more, seeded so a rerun gives the same groups. A group is named by the definitions common inside it and uncommon outside it. Groups of fewer than three are not listed.

    Same statement up to numbers and names compares a fingerprint Lean computes from each elaborated target, with local definitions unfolded and numerals, universe levels, binder names and metadata erased. Same template also erases every type, definition, predicate and instance, keeping only the logic (∧, ∃, =, ≤, +, ∈), so it groups questions of one shape about different objects.

    Checked by Lean puts two statements side by side in one Lean file and asks the kernel to accept claim A → claim B with a short tactic suite. Proved means the file elaborated and the theorem reaches no axiom beyond propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. Candidates are pairs with the same fingerprint, the same template and similar vocabulary, or the nearest vocabulary neighbours. What is proved relates two Lean statements; whether it relates the problems as posed waits on a person reading the statements.

    A problem's name is built from its source id, and the text under it is the prose its folder publishes. The number is its MathDB problem number. The page is generated by the mathdb-lean library's tools/vocabulary.py and is not edited by hand.
